steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write a short introduction for our paper presenting AutoPrognosis 2.0, our automated machine learning tool for diagnostic and prognostic modeling in healthcare. Cover why ML is still hard for clinicians to use, our earlier AutoPrognosis work, what the new version can do, and what the rest of the paper contains.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Machine learning (ML) systems could revolutionize medicine and become core clinical tools. But there are many different challenges that have to be overcome before ML is adopted routinely and widely. In particular, there are big technical challenges in developing, understanding and deploying ML systems, and right now these make them mostly inaccessible to medical practitioners.

To try to address this, we previously developed AutoPrognosis, an automated machine learning (AutoML) framework for training predictive models. Since then the framework has been used to derive prognostic models for cardiovascular disease, cystic fibrosis and breast cancer, and also for a number of other indications. However, our first approach had significant limitations, both algorithmic ones and ones in terms of usability.

So in this work we describe AutoPrognosis 2.0. It addresses all the major obstacles that limit the development, interpretation and deployment of ML methods in medicine, and it is a step-change in diagnostic and prognostic modeling. We believe it is the world's first method that can do all of these things at the same time: (1) solve classification, regression and time-to-event problems; (2) optimize ML pipelines, find the most appropriate models and tune hyperparameters automatically; (3) identify key variables and novel risk factors, so that clinicians can select different numbers of variables and understand the value of information; (4) give many kinds of model explanations, including feature-based ones, example-based ones and closed-form risk equations; and (5) produce web-based applications so models can easily be shared with the clinical community.

In this paper we first outline the major challenges for the clinical development and translation of diagnostic and prognostic modeling. Then we describe our approach, AutoPrognosis 2.0, and explain how it addresses each of the challenges. Finally we show AutoPrognosis 2.0 applied in an illustrative scenario, which is prognostic risk prediction of diabetes using a cohort of 502,467 individuals from UK Biobank. But AutoPrognosis can be used to build diagnostic and prognostic models for any disease or clinical outcome, and it is explicitly designed so that people who are not ML experts can build models. We have open-sourced AutoPrognosis 2.0 as a tool for the community, so that clinicians or non-expert users can use the automated framework to develop optimized personalized diagnostics, prognostics and risk scores with modern machine learning techniques in a robust and reproducible way.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Machine learning (ML) systems have the potential to revolutionize medicine and become core clinical tools [1]. However, there is a diverse set of challenges that must be overcome before routine and widespread ML adoption [2,3]. In particular, there are substantial technical challenges in developing, understanding, and deploying ML systems, which currently make them largely inaccessible for medical practitioners [3,4,5,6].

In an attempt to address this, we previously developed AutoPrognosis, an automated machine learning (AutoML) framework to train predictive models [7]. This framework has since been applied to derive prognostic models for cardiovascular disease [8], cystic fibrosis [9], and breast cancer [10], among a number of other indications [11,12,13,14,15,16]. However, our initial approach had significant limitations from both an algorithmic and a usability perspective.

Consequently, in this work we describe AutoPrognosis 2.0, which addresses all major obstacles limiting the development, interpretation and deployment of ML methods in medicine and represents a step-change in diagnostic and prognostic modeling. In particular, we believe this is the world's first method that can simultaneously: (1) solve classification, regression, and time-to-event problems; (2) optimize ML pipelines, determine the most appropriate models, and automatically tune hyperparameters; (3) identify key variables and novel risk factors, allowing clinicians to select different numbers of variables and understand the value of information; (4) provide a diverse range of model explanations, including feature-based, example-based, and closed-form risk equations; and (5) produce web-based applications, so that models can be readily shared with the clinical community.

In this paper, we outline the major challenges facing clinical development and translation of diagnostic and prognostic modeling. We then describe our approach, AutoPrognosis 2.0, and detail how it addresses each challenge. Finally, we demonstrate AutoPrognosis 2.0 in an illustrative scenario: prognostic risk prediction of diabetes using a cohort of 502,467 individuals from UK Biobank. We emphasize, however, that AutoPrognosis can be applied to construct diagnostic and prognostic models for any disease or clinical outcome, and is explicitly designed to make model building accessible to non-ML experts. We have open-sourced AutoPrognosis 2.0 as a tool for the community, allowing clinicians or non-expert users to adopt the automated framework to robustly and reproducibly develop optimized personalized diagnostics, prognostics, and risk scores using modern machine learning techniques.
